question.text:
\[ P= \begin{bmatrix} 0.3 & 0.8 \\ 0.7 & 0.2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{q}= \begin{bmatrix} 0.1 \\ 0.9 \end{bmatrix} \]

Consider the stochastic matrix $P$ and vector $\mathbf{q}$ shown above. Which of the following statements are true?

  1. $\mathbf{q}$ is a stochastic vector
  2. $P\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{q}$
  3. $\mathbf{q}$ is a steady-state vector of $P$
question.choice4: None of the statements are true
question.explanation:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $\mathbf{q}$ such that $P\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{q}.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

  • Statement I is true. Indeed, $\mathbf{q}$ is a stochastic vector since its entries are non-negative and add up to $1.$

  • Statement II is false. Note that \[ P\mathbf{q} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.3 & 0.8 \\ 0.7 & 0.2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0.1 \\ 0.9 \end{bmatrix} =\begin{bmatrix} 0.03 + 0.72 \\ 0.07+0.18 \end{bmatrix} =\begin{bmatrix} 0.75 \\ 0.25 \end{bmatrix} \neq\mathbf{q}. \]

  • Statement III is false. Since $P\mathbf{q}\neq\mathbf{q},$ it is not a steady-state vector of $P.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

exampleAnswers.title: Finding the Steady-State Vector of a Stochastic 2x2 Matrix

question.text:
\[ P= \begin{bmatrix} 0.4 & 0.1 \\ 0.6 & 0.9 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{q}= \begin{bmatrix} {a} \\ {b} \end{bmatrix} \]

Given that $\mathbf{q}$ is the steady-state vector of the stochastic matrix $P,$ what is the value of $a-b?$
question.explanation:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $\mathbf{q}$ such that

\begin{align*} P\mathbf{q} &= \mathbf{q} \\[5pt] P\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{q} &= \mathbf{0} \\[5pt] P\mathbf{q} - I\mathbf{q} &= \mathbf{0} \\[5pt] (P - I)\mathbf{q} &= \mathbf{0}. \end{align*}

Computing $P-I,$ we get

\[ P-I = \begin{bmatrix} 0.4 & 0.1 \\ 0.6 & 0.9 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -0.6 & 0.1 \\ 0.6 & -0.1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The matrix equation $(P-I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0}$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

\begin{align*} M &= \left[ \begin{array}{cc|c} -0.6 & 0.1 & 0 \\ 0.6 & -0.1 & 0 \end{array} \right] & R_2 & := R_2 + R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{cc|c} -0.6 & 0.1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{array} \right] \end{align*}

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain

\[ x_1=\dfrac{1}{6}x_2. \]

Hence, the general solution is

\[ \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{6}x_2 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x_2 \in \mathbb{R}. \]

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have

\begin{align*} \dfrac{1}{6}x_2 + x_2 &= 1 \\[5pt] \dfrac{7}{6}x_2 &= 1 \\[5pt] x_2 &= \dfrac{6}{7}. \end{align*}

Therefore,

\[ \mathbf{q}= \begin{bmatrix} a \\ b \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{7} \\ \dfrac{6}{7} \end{bmatrix}. \]

Finally, $a-b=\dfrac{1}{7}-\dfrac{6}{7} = -\dfrac{5}{7}.$

question.text:
There are two groups of people In a small town: those who travel to work by car and those who travel by train. Every year a study is done in which people are asked about their preference between using trains versus cars. The table below shows the results of this study.

From:
Car Train
To: Car $0.35$ $0.25$
Train $0.65$ $0.75$

It's found that $65 \%$ of people who currently travel by car will switch to train next year, while $25\%$ of people who currently travel by train will switch to their car next year.

Assuming that the town has $90\,000$ people that travel to work by train or car, and the given probabilities remain constant over many years, how many people will eventually use the train to travel to work?
question.explanation:
From the table, we get the corresponding stochastic matrix \[ P= \begin{bmatrix} 0.35 & 0.25 \\ 0.65 & 0.75 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Notice that $P$ contains only positive entries. So, the matrix $P$ is regular. As a result, after many years, the distribution will eventually converge to the unique steady-state vector of $P,$ and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $\mathbf{q}$ such that

\begin{align*} P\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{q} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad (P - I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0}. \end{align*}

Computing $P-I,$ we get

\[ P-I = \begin{bmatrix} 0.35 & 0.25 \\ 0.65 & 0.75 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -0.65 & 0.25 \\ 0.65 & -0.25 \end{bmatrix}. \]

So, the matrix equation $(P-I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0}$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

\begin{align*} M &= \left[ \begin{array}{cc|c} -0.65 & 0.25 & 0 \\ 0.65 & -0.25 & 0 \end{array} \right] & R_2 & := R_2 + R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{cc|c} -0.65 & 0.25 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{array} \right] \end{align*}

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain \begin{align} x_1 = \dfrac{5}{13}x_2. \end{align}

Hence, the general solution is \[ \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{5}{13}x_2 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x_2 \in \mathbb{R}. \]

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have \begin{align*} \dfrac{5}{13}x_2 + x_2 & = 1 \\[5pt] \dfrac{18}{13}x_2 & = 1 \\[5pt] x_2 & = \dfrac{13}{18}. \end{align*}

Therefore, \[ \mathbf{q} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{5}{18} \\ {\color{blue}{\dfrac{13}{18}}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

So, ${\color{blue}{\dfrac{13}{18}}}$ of the people will eventually use the train to travel. Therefore, the number of people who will eventually use the train is \[ \dfrac{13}{18} \cdot 90\,000 = 65\,000. \]

question.text:
\[ P= \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0.3 \\ 1 & 0.7 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{q}= \begin{bmatrix} {a} \\ {b} \end{bmatrix} \]

Given that $\mathbf{q}$ is the steady-state vector of the stochastic matrix $P,$ what is the value of $a-b?$
question.explanation:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $\mathbf{q}$ such that

\begin{align*} P\mathbf{q} &= \mathbf{q} \\[5pt] P\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{q} &= \mathbf{0} \\[5pt] P\mathbf{q} - I\mathbf{q} &= \mathbf{0} \\[5pt] (P - I)\mathbf{q} &= \mathbf{0}. \end{align*}

Computing $P-I,$ we get

\[ P-I = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0.3 \\ 1 & 0.7 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0.3 \\ 1 & -0.3 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The matrix equation $(P-I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0}$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

\begin{align*} M &= \left[ \begin{array}{cc|c} -1 & 0.3 & 0 \\ 1 & -0.3 & 0 \end{array} \right] & R_2 & := R_2 + R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{cc|c} -1 & 0.3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{array} \right] \end{align*}

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain \begin{align} -x_1 + 0.3x_2 & = 0\\[5pt] 10x_1 - 3x_2 & = 0\\[5pt] x_1 & = \dfrac{3}{10}x_2 \end{align}

Hence, the general solution is \[ \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{3}{10}x_2 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x_2 \in \mathbb{R}. \]

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have

\begin{align*} \dfrac{3}{10}x_2 + x_2 & = 1 \\[5pt] \dfrac{13}{10}x_2 & = 1 \\[5pt] x_2 &= \dfrac{10}{13}. \end{align*}

Therefore,

\[ \mathbf{q}= \begin{bmatrix} a \\ b \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{3}{13} \\ \dfrac{10}{13} \end{bmatrix}. \]

Finally, $a - b = \dfrac{3}{13} - \dfrac{10}{13} = -\dfrac{7}{13}.$

\[ P= \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0.6 \\ 1 & 0.4 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{q}= \begin{bmatrix} {a} \\ {b} \end{bmatrix} \]

Given that $\mathbf{q}$ is the steady-state vector of the stochastic matrix $P,$ what is the value of $a-b?$

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $\mathbf{q}$ such that

\begin{align*} P\mathbf{q} &= \mathbf{q} \\[5pt] P\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{q} &= \mathbf{0} \\[5pt] P\mathbf{q} - I\mathbf{q} &= \mathbf{0} \\[5pt] (P - I)\mathbf{q} &= \mathbf{0}. \end{align*}

Computing $P-I,$ we get

\[ P-I = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0.6 \\ 1 & 0.4 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0.6 \\ 1 & -0.6 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The matrix equation $(P-I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0}$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

\begin{align*} M &= \left[ \begin{array}{cc|c} -1 & 0.6 & 0 \\ 1 & -0.6 & 0 \end{array} \right] & R_2 & := R_2 + R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{cc|c} -1 & 0.6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{array} \right] \end{align*}

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain \begin{align} -x_1 + 0.6x_2 & = 0\\[5pt] -x_1 +\dfrac{3}{5}x_2 & = 0\\[5pt] x_1 & = \dfrac{3}{5}x_2 \end{align}

Hence, the general solution is \[ \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{3}{5}x_2 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x_2 \in \mathbb{R}. \]

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have

\begin{align*} \dfrac{3}{5}x_2 + x_2 & = 1 \\[5pt] \dfrac{8}{5}x_2 & = 1 \\[5pt] x_2 &= \dfrac{5}{8}. \end{align*}

Therefore,

\[ \mathbf{q}= \begin{bmatrix} a \\ b \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{3}{8} \\ \dfrac{5}{8} \end{bmatrix}. \]

Finally, $a - b = \dfrac{3}{8} - \dfrac{5}{8} = -\dfrac{1}{4}.$

question.text:
The migration table below describes the movement of the population between cities and suburbs every year in a certain state.

From:
Cities Suburbs
To: Cities $0.8$ $0.7$
Suburbs $0.2$ $0.3$

That is, $20\%$ of those living in cities move to the suburbs each year, and $70\%$ of those living in suburbs move to the cities.

Assuming that the population of the state is $9$ million and remains constant, how many people would eventually live in cities if the given probabilities remain constant over many years?
question.explanation:
From the table, we get the corresponding stochastic matrix

\[ P= \begin{bmatrix} 0.8 & 0.7 \\ 0.2 & 0.3 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Notice that $P$ contains only positive entries. So, the matrix $P$ is regular. As a result, after many years, the distribution will eventually converge to the unique steady-state vector of $P,$ and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $\mathbf{q}$ such that

\begin{align*} P\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{q} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad (P - I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0}. \end{align*}

Computing $P-I,$ we get

\[ P-I = \begin{bmatrix} 0.8 & 0.7 \\ 0.2 & 0.3 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -0.2 & 0.7 \\ 0.2 & -0.7 \end{bmatrix}. \]

So, the matrix equation $(P-I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0}$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

\begin{align*} M &= \left[ \begin{array}{cc|c} -0.2 & 0.7 & 0 \\ 0.2 & -0.7 & 0 \end{array} \right] & R_2 & := R_2 + R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{cc|c} -0.2 & 0.7 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{array} \right] \end{align*}

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain

\[ x_1=\dfrac{7}{2}x_2. \]

Hence, the general solution is

\[ \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{7}{2}x_2 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x_2 \in \mathbb{R}. \]

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have

\begin{align*} \dfrac{7}{2}x_2 + x_2 &= 1 \\[5pt] \dfrac{9}{2}x_2 &= 1 \\[5pt] x_2 &= \dfrac{2}{9}. \end{align*}

Therefore,

\[ \mathbf{q} = \begin{bmatrix} {\color{blue}{\dfrac{7}{9}}} \\ \dfrac{2}{9} \end{bmatrix}. \]

So, after many years, ${\color{blue}{\dfrac{7}{9}}} $ of the $9$ million population will live in cities. Therefore, the total number of people living in cities after many years will be

\[ \dfrac{7}{9} \cdot 9\,\textrm{million} = 7 \,\textrm{million}. \]

exampleAnswers.title: Finding the Steady-State Vector of a Stochastic 3x3 Matrix

question.text:
\[ P= \begin{bmatrix} 0.1 & 0.4 & 0.5 \\ 0.6 & 0.1 & 0.3 \\ 0.3 & 0.5 & 0.2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{q}= \begin{bmatrix} {a} \\ {b} \\ {c} \end{bmatrix} \]

Given that $\mathbf{q}$ is the steady-state vector of the stochastic matrix $P$ shown above, what is the value of $a+b-c?$
question.explanation:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $\mathbf{q}$ such that

\begin{align*} P\mathbf{q} &= \mathbf{q} \\[3pt] P\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{q} &= \mathbf{0} \\[3pt] P\mathbf{q} - I\mathbf{q} &= \mathbf{0} \\[3pt] (P - I)\mathbf{q} &= \mathbf{0}. \end{align*}

Computing $P-I,$ we get

\[ P-I = \begin{bmatrix} 0.1 & 0.4 & 0.5 \\ 0.6 & 0.1 & 0.3 \\ 0.3 & 0.5 & 0.2 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -0.9 & 0.4 & 0.5 \\ 0.6 & -0.9 & 0.3 \\ 0.3 & 0.5 & -0.8 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The matrix equation $(P-I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0}$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

\begin{align*} M &= \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c} -0.9 & 0.4 & 0.5 & 0 \\ 0.6 & -0.9 & 0.3 & 0 \\ 0.3 & 0.5 & -0.8 & 0 \end{array} \right] && \begin{array}{l} R_1 := 10R_1 \\ R_2 := 10R_2 \\ R_3 := 10R_3 \\ \end{array} \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c} -9 & 4 & 5 & 0 \\ 6 & -9 & 3 & 0 \\ 3 & 5 & -8 & 0 \end{array} \right] && \begin{array}{l} R_3 \leftrightarrow R_1 \\ \end{array} \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c} 3 & 5 & -8 & 0 \\ 6 & -9 & 3 & 0 \\ -9 & 4 & 5 & 0 \end{array} \right] && \begin{array}{l} R_2 := R_2 - 2R_1 \\ R_3 := R_3 + 3R_1 \\ \end{array} \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c} 3 & 5 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & -19 & 19 & 0 \\ 0 & 19 & -19 & 0 \end{array} \right] && \begin{array}{l} R_3 := R_3 + R_2 \end{array} \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c} 3 & 5 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & -19 & 19 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{array} \right] \end{align*}

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, $x_3$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain \[ x_2 = x_3. \] Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain \[ 3x_1 + 5x_3 - 8x_3 = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x_1 = x_3. \] Hence, the general solution is \[ \begin{bmatrix} x_3 \\ x_3 \\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x_3 \in \mathbb{R}. \]

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have \begin{align*} x_3 + x_3 + x_3 & = 1 \\[5pt] 3x_3 &= 1 \\[5pt] x_3 & = \dfrac{1}{3}. \end{align*}

Therefore, \[ \mathbf{q}= \begin{bmatrix} a \\ b \\ c \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{3} \\ \dfrac{1}{3} \\ \dfrac{1}{3} \end{bmatrix}. \]

Finally, \[ a + b - c = \dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{1}{3} - \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{1}{3}. \]

\begin{align*} P\mathbf{q} &= \mathbf{q} \\[3pt] P\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{q} &= \mathbf{0} \\[3pt] P\mathbf{q} - I\mathbf{q} &= \mathbf{0} \\[3pt] (P - I)\mathbf{q} &= \mathbf{0}. \end{align*}

Computing $P-I,$ we get

\[ P-I = \begin{bmatrix} 0.4 & 0.4 & 0.4 \\ 0.4 & 0.4 & 0.2 \\ 0.2 & 0.2 & 0.4 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -0.6 & 0.4 & 0.4 \\ 0.4 & -0.6 & 0.2 \\ 0.2 & 0.2 & -0.6 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The matrix equation $(P-I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0}$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

\begin{align*} M &= \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c} -0.6 & 0.4 & 0.4 & 0 \\ 0.4 & -0.6 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0.2 & 0.2 & -0.6& 0 \end{array} \right] && \begin{array}{l} R_1 := 10R_1 \\ R_2 := 10R_2 \\ R_3 := 10R_3 \\ \end{array} \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c} -6 & 4 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & -6 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 & -6& 0 \end{array} \right] && \begin{array}{l} R_3 \leftrightarrow R_1 \\ \end{array} \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c} 2 & 2 & -6& 0 \\ 4 & -6 & 2 & 0 \\ -6 & 4 & 4 & 0 \end{array} \right] && \begin{array}{l} R_2 := R_2 - 2R_1 \\ R_3 := R_3 + 3R_1 \\ \end{array} \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c} 2 & 2 & -6& 0 \\ 0 & -10 & 14 & 0 \\ 0 & 10 & -14 & 0 \\ \end{array} \right] && \begin{array}{l} R_3 := R_3 + R_2 \end{array} \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c} 2 & 2 & -6& 0 \\ 0 & -10 & 14 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ \end{array} \right] \end{align*}

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, $x_3$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain \[ x_2 = \dfrac{14}{10}x_3 = \dfrac 75 x_3. \] Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain \[ 2x_1 + 2\left(\dfrac 75 x_3\right) - 6x_3 = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x_1 = \dfrac{8}{5}x_3. \] Hence, the general solution is \[ \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{8}{5}x_3 \\ \dfrac 75 x_3 \\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x_3 \in \mathbb{R}. \]

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have \begin{align*} \dfrac{8}{5}x_3 + \dfrac{7}{5}x_3 + x_3 & = 1 \\[5pt] \dfrac{20}{5}x_3 &= 1 \\[5pt] x_3 & = \dfrac{1}{4}. \end{align*}

Therefore, \[ \mathbf{q}= \begin{bmatrix} a \\ b \\ c \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2}{5} \\ \dfrac{7}{20} \\ \dfrac{1}{4} \end{bmatrix}. \]

Finally, \[ a + b - c = \dfrac{2}{5} + \dfrac{7}{20} - \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{10}{20} = \dfrac{1}{2}. \]

example.title: Finding the Steady-State Vector of a Stochastic 3x3 Matrix

question.text:
\[ P= \begin{bmatrix} 0.4 & 0.2 & 0.1 \\ 0.3 & 0.2 & 0.65 \\ 0.3 & 0.6 & 0.25 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{q}= \begin{bmatrix} {a} \\ {b} \\ {c} \end{bmatrix} \]

Given that $\mathbf{q}$ is the steady-state vector of the stochastic matrix $P$ shown above, what is the value of $a+b-c?$
question.explanation:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $\mathbf{q}$ such that

\begin{align*} P\mathbf{q} &= \mathbf{q} \\[3pt] P\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{q} &= \mathbf{0} \\[3pt] P\mathbf{q} - I\mathbf{q} &= \mathbf{0} \\[3pt] (P - I)\mathbf{q} &= \mathbf{0}. \end{align*}

Computing $P-I,$ we get

\[ P-I = \begin{bmatrix} 0.4 & 0.2 & 0.1 \\ 0.3 & 0.2 & 0.65 \\ 0.3 & 0.6 & 0.25 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -0.6 & 0.2 & 0.1 \\ 0.3 & -0.8 & 0.65 \\ 0.3 & 0.6 & -0.75 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The matrix equation $(P-I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0}$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

\begin{align*} M &= \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c} -0.6 & 0.2 & 0.1 & 0 \\ 0.3 & -0.8 & 0.65 & 0 \\ 0.3 & 0.6 & -0.75 & 0 \end{array} \right] && \begin{array}{l} R_1 := 5R_1 \\ R_2 := 10R_2 \\ R_3 := 10R_3 \\ \end{array} \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c} -3 & 1 & 0.5 & 0 \\ 3 & -8 & 6.5 & 0 \\ 3 & 6 & -7.5 & 0 \end{array} \right] && \begin{array}{l} R_2 := R_2 +R_1 \\ R_3 := R_3 +R_1 \\ \end{array} \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c} -3 & 1 & 0.5 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 7 & -7 & 0 \end{array} \right] && \begin{array}{l} R_3 := R_3 + R_2 \\ \end{array} \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c} -3 & 1 & 0.5 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{array} \right] \end{align*}

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, $x_3$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain \[ x_2 = x_3. \] Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain \[ -3x_1 + x_3 + 0.5x_3 = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x_1 = \dfrac{1}{2}x_3. \] Hence, the general solution is

\[ \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{2}x_3 \\ x_3 \\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x_3 \in \mathbb{R}. \]

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have \begin{align*} \dfrac{1}{2}x_3 + x_3 + x_3 &= 1 \\[5pt] \dfrac{5}{2}x_3 &= 1 \\[5pt] x_3 & = \dfrac{2}{5}. \end{align*}

Therefore, \[ \mathbf{q}= \begin{bmatrix} a \\ b \\ c \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{5} \\ \dfrac{2}{5} \\ \dfrac{2}{5} \end{bmatrix}. \]

Finally, \[ a + b - c = \dfrac{1}{5} + \dfrac{2}{5} - \dfrac{2}{5} = \dfrac{1}{5}. \]

example.title: Finding the Steady-State Vector of a Stochastic 3x3 Matrix

question.text:
A study shows how the sports preferences of young people in a certain community vary from year to year. The following table shows the results of this study.

From:
Baseball Basketball Football
To: Baseball $0.8$ $0.2$ $0$
Basketball $0.1$ $0.6$ $0.2$
Football $0.1$ $0.2$ $0.8$

For example, $10 \%$ of people who used to prefer baseball now prefer football.

Given that $1\,260$ young people were interviewed for the study and that the probabilities listed remain constant for many years, how many of those people will eventually prefer baseball?
question.explanation:
From the table, we get the corresponding stochastic matrix

\[ P= \begin{bmatrix} 0.8 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0.1 & 0.6 & 0.2 \\ 0.1 & 0.2 & 0.8 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Notice that the matrix $P^2$ contains only positive entries. So, the matrix $P$ is regular. As a result, after many years, the distribution will eventually converge to the steady-state vector of $P,$ and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $\mathbf{q}$ such that

\begin{align*} P\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{q} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad (P - I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0}. \end{align*}

Computing $P-I,$ we get

\[ P-I = \begin{bmatrix} 0.8 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0.1 & 0.6 & 0.2 \\ 0.1 & 0.2 & 0.8 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -0.2 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0.1 & -0.4 & 0.2 \\ 0.1 & 0.2 & -0.2 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The matrix equation $(P-I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0}$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

\begin{align*} M &= \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c} -0.2 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0.1 & -0.4 & 0.2 \\ 0.1 & 0.2 & -0.2 \end{array} \right] && \begin{array}{l} R_1 := -5R_1 \\ R_2 := 10R_2 \\ R_3 := 10R_3 \\ \end{array} \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & -4 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & -2 & 0 \end{array} \right] && \begin{array}{l} R_2 := R_2 +(-1)R_1 \\ R_3 := R_3 +(-1)R_1 \end{array} \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -2 & 0 \end{array} \right] && \begin{array}{l} R_3 := R_3 +R_2 \\ \end{array} \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{array} \right] \end{align*}

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, $x_3$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain \[ x_2 = \dfrac{2}{3}x_3. \] Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

\[x_1 - \dfrac{2}{3}x_3 + 0x_3 = 0 \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad x_1 = \dfrac{2}{3}x_3. \]

Hence, the general solution is \[ \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2}{3}x_3 \\ \dfrac{2}{3}x_3 \\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x_3 \in \mathbb{R}. \]

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have

\begin{align*} \dfrac{2}{3}x_3 + \dfrac{2}{3}x_3 + x_3 & = 1 \\[5pt] \dfrac{7}{3}x_3 &= 1 \\[5pt] x_3 &= \dfrac{3}{7}. \end{align*}

Therefore,

\[ \mathbf{q} = \begin{bmatrix} \color{blue}\dfrac{2}{7} \\ {{\dfrac{2}{7}}} \\ \dfrac{3}{7} \end{bmatrix}. \]

So, after many years, ${\color{blue}{\dfrac{2}{7}}}$ of the people will prefer baseball. Therefore, the number of people who will prefer baseball is \[ \dfrac{2}{7} \cdot 1\,260 = 360 \, \textrm{people}. \]

example.title: Finding the Steady-State Vector of a Stochastic 3x3 Matrix

question.text:
A study conducted on $3\,400$ teenagers by the transportation department of a particular city reveals that teenagers' preference for the type of home-to-school transportation changes with time. The following table shows the results of this study.

From:
Bus Bicycle Electric Scooter
To: Bus $0.2$ $0.2$ $0$
Bicycle $0.4$ $0.4$ $0.4$
Electric Scooter $0.4$ $0.4$ $0.6$

For example, $40\%$ of teenagers who used to go to school by bus now go by bicycle.

How many teenagers would eventually go to school on electric scooters if the listed probabilities remained constant over many years?
question.explanation:
From the table, we get the corresponding stochastic matrix

\[ P= \begin{bmatrix} 0.2 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0.4 & 0.4 & 0.4 \\ 0.4 & 0.4 & 0.6 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Notice that the matrix $P^2$ contains only positive entries. So, the matrix $P$ is regular. As a result, after many years, the distribution will eventually converge to the steady-state vector of $P,$ and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $\mathbf{q}$ such that

\begin{align*} P\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{q} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad (P - I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0}. \end{align*}

Computing $P-I,$ we get

\[ P-I = \begin{bmatrix} 0.2 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0.4 & 0.4 & 0.4 \\ 0.4 & 0.4 & 0.6 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -0.8 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0.4 & -0.6 & 0.4 \\ 0.4 & 0.4 & -0.4 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The matrix equation $(P-I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0}$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

\begin{align*} M &= \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c} -0.8 & 0.2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0.4 & -0.6 & 0.4 & 0 \\ 0.4 & 0.4 & -0.4 &0 \end{array} \right] && \begin{array}{l} R_1 := 5R_1 \\ R_2 := 5R_2 \\ R_3 := \dfrac52R_3 \\ \end{array} \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c} -4 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 &- 3 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -1 & 0 \end{array} \right] && \begin{array}{l} R_1\leftrightarrow R_3 \\ \end{array} \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 2 &- 3 & 2 & 0 \\ -4 & 1 & 0 & 0 \end{array} \right] && \begin{array}{l} R_2 := R_2 +(-2)R_1 \\ R_3 := R_3 +4R_1 \\ \end{array} \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & -4 & 0 \end{array} \right] && \begin{array}{l} R_3 := R_2 + R_3 \\ \end{array} \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{array} \right] \end{align*}

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, $x_3$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain \[ x_2=\dfrac45 x_3. \] Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain \[ x_1+\left(\dfrac45x_3\right)-x_3 = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x_1=\dfrac15x_3. \] Hence, the general solution is

\[ \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac15 x_3 \\ \dfrac45x_3 \\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x_3 \in \mathbb{R}. \]

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have

\begin{align*} \dfrac15 x_3 +\dfrac45 x_3+x_3 &= 1 \\[5pt] 2x_3 &= 1 \\[5pt] x_3 &= \dfrac{1}{2}. \end{align*}

Therefore,

\[ \mathbf{q} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{10} \\ \dfrac{4}{10} \\ {\color{blue}{\dfrac{1}{2}}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

So, after many years, ${\color{blue}{\dfrac{1}{2}}}$ of the teenagers will go to school in electric scooters. Therefore, the total number of teenagers in the city that will go to school in electric scooters will be

\[ \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot 3\,400= 1\, 700. \]
